record.description: Melito of Sardis' Paschal Homily (c. 160-170 CE) is the most Pauline of second-century texts on sin and freedom. Pasch. 47-49 presents anthropology of original capability: humans were "by nature capable of receiving good and evil" (φύσει δεκτικὸς ὤν ἀγαθοῦ καὶ πονηροῦ). Pasch. 49-54 describes radical post-lapsarian condition: Adam's "inheritance" (κληρονομία) includes servitude not freedom (οὐκ ἐλευθερίαν ἀλλὰ δουλείαν); humanity is "snatched by tyrannical sin" (ἀνηρπάζοντο ὑπὸ τῆς τυραννικῆς ἁμαρτίας). The Sin-Death alliance is personified (ἡ τοῦ θανάτου συνεργός). More pessimistic than Justin/Tatian, closer to Paul. Critical edition: Perler (SC 123, 1966).
record.label: On the Pascha (Περὶ Πάσχα)

record.description: Syriac dialogue attributed to Bardesanes of Edessa, composed according to the communis opinio by his disciple Philip toward the beginning of the third century (probably before 222, the date of Bardesanes’ death). The oldest surviving monument of Syriac literature outside biblical translations. The dialogue, originally entitled Dialogue on Fate (peri heimarmenes), depicts the ageing Bardesanes discussing with his disciples Awida, Schemaschgram, Philip, and Bar-Yamma the reconciliation of astrological fatalism and human freedom. For Amand 1945 (Book II ch. III, p. 229-257), the work is a crucial secondary witness to the Carneadean tradition: Bardesanes deploys there, with unprecedented ethnographic profusion, the argument of the nomima barbarika, and reproduces several other Neo-Academic topoi. The threefold delimitation physis / heimarmene / autexousion structures the entire dialogue. Eusebius PE VI.10 cites lengthy extracts from the Greek translation, and the pseudo-Clementine Recognitiones IX.19-28 as well as pseudo-Caesarius Quaest. 109-110 likewise derive from it.
record.label: Bardesane (et Philippe), Le Livre des lois des pays (Liber Legum Regionum)

metadata.description_fr: Dialogue syriaque attribue a Bardesane d'Edesse, redige selon la communis opinio par son disciple Philippe vers le debut du IIIe siecle (probablement avant 222, mort de Bardesane). Le dialogue, originellement intitule Dialogue sur le Destin (peri heimarmenes), met en scene Bardesane vieillissant discutant avec ses disciples Awida, Schemaschgram, Philippe et Bar-Yamma de la conciliation entre fatalisme astrologique et liberte humaine. Pour Amand 1945 (Livre II Ch. La triple delimitation physis / heimarmene / autexousion structure tout le dialogue. Eusebe PE VI.10 cite de longs extraits de la traduction grecque, et les Recognitiones pseudo-clementines IX.19-28 ainsi que le pseudo-Cesaire Quaest. 109-110 en derivent egalement

record.description:
Embassy for the Christians (Πρεσβεία περὶ Χριστιανῶν), an apologetic address composed c. 177 CE and presented to Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Aurelius Commodus (co-emperor). The work defends Christians against charges of atheism, Thyestean feasts, and Oedipean unions.

The philosophically significant section for free will falls at ch. 24.3–6. Athenagoras constructs a parallel between human moral freedom and angelic freedom to explain evil without impugning divine providence. In 24.4 he states that humans have virtue and vice αὐθαίρετον ("by self-chosen disposition"), grounding moral responsibility in the self-chosen character of action. In 24.5 the same term governs angels: αὐθαίρετοι δὴ γεγόνασιν ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ ("they were created self-determining by God"), explaining the angelic fall as the exercise of created freedom, not divine causation.

Terminological note: Athenagoras consistently uses αὐθαίρετον, not αὐτεξούσιον (confirmed absent from the text). This is a significant second-century distinction: αὐθαίρετον emphasizes the self-chosen quality of an act, while αὐτεξούσιον (dominant from Origen onwards) emphasizes the power of self-determination. Εἱμαρμένη appears only once (Legatio 6.5, καθ' εἱμαρμένην), within a doxographical report of Stoic physics, not in the free-will section (ch. 24). Editions: Schoedel OECT (1972); Pouderon SC 379 (1992).
record.label: Legatio pro Christianis (SC 379)

record.description: Monograph by Paul Linjamaa (Brill 2019, *Nag Hammadi and Manichaean Studies* 95, xii+352 p.) devoted to the ethics of the *Traité Tripartite* (NHC I, 5)—a Valentinian Coptic text discovered at Nag Hammadi (Codex Jung). Linjamaa analyses how the pneumatic / psychic / hylic tripartition of human souls, traditionally read as "deterministic" (salvation would be pre-assigned by nature), in fact accommodates a form of conditional free will. A new reference on Gnostic-Valentinian determinism, relevant to the debate with Origen and Clement of Alexandria.

record.description: Epideixis tou apostolikou kerygmatos, a short catechetical treatise by Irenaeus of Lyons. Known only through an Armenian translation discovered in 1904. For Amand 1945 (Book II ch. II, p. 213, 215), the work complements the Adversus Haereses as a synthetic exposition of the 'rule of faith' (kanon tes aletheias). Standard edition: K. Ter-Mekerttschian and S. G. Wilson in the Patrologia Orientalis XII fasc. 5 (Firmin-Didot, Paris 1919) p. 663-664. It has no direct connection with the anti-fatalist argumentation, but is useful for the Irenaean theodicy of divine free will

record.description: Article by James E. Tomberlin and Frank McGuinness (*Religious Studies* 13/4, 1977, p. 455-475) examining and formally reconstructing Alvin Plantinga’s *Free Will Defence* (developed in *God and Other Minds* 1967 and *The Nature of Necessity* 1974, and popularized in *God, Freedom, and Evil* Eerdmans 1974/1977). The Free Will Defence seeks to demonstrate the logical consistency between (1) the existence of an omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good God and (2) the existence of moral evil, through the hypothesis of *transworld depravity* and creaturely libertarian freedom. Canonical KG reference for analytic theodicy.
record.label: Tomberlin, J.E. & McGuinness, F. (1977). God, Evil, and the Free Will Defence. Religious Studies 13: 455-475. [Reviewing Plantinga's argument]

metadata.description_fr: Article de James E. Tomberlin et Frank McGuinness (*Religious Studies* 13/4, 1977, p. 455-475) examinant et reconstruisant formellement la *Free Will Defence* d'Alvin Plantinga (développée dans *God and Other Minds* 1967 et *The Nature of Necessity* 1974, et popularisée dans *God, Freedom, and Evil* Eerdmans 1974/1977). Référence canonique du KG pour la théodicée analytique.
